opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the central questions as we move from talking to a single chatbot toward a world where you might have thousands or millions of AI instances doing real work: writing code, running experiments, maybe doing a lot of the alignment research itself.

The core difficulty is that human supervision doesn't scale the way the workforce does. If you have a million copies of a model each doing hours of work a day, there's no way humans can look at everything. And increasingly the work will be things we can't easily evaluate even if we did look: a giant pull request, a subtle research result, a complicated plan. So the question becomes how you stay in control when you can only spot-check a tiny fraction, and when the things you're checking may be beyond your ability to judge directly.

I think about it as a few layers. The first is scalable oversight: using AI to help humans evaluate AI. If one model writes code, another model can critique it, point out bugs, and flag suspicious parts, so the human reviewer is much more effective than they'd be alone. The bet is that evaluation is easier than generation, so you can leverage that asymmetry. But you then have to worry about whether the assistants are themselves trustworthy, and whether models could collude.

The second layer is having stronger insight into what's going on inside the models: interpretability, but also simpler things like monitoring chain-of-thought reasoning while that still reflects what the model is actually doing. If you can catch a model reasoning about deceiving its overseers, that's extremely valuable.

The third is control-style thinking: assume some fraction of your workforce might be misaligned, and design the system so that it still can't do catastrophic damage. Limited permissions, audit logs, having untrusted outputs reviewed by trusted weaker models, red-teaming your own setup. It's similar to how you'd run a large organization where you can't vet every employee perfectly.

And then fundamentally you want to actually make the models aligned in the first place, so you're not relying purely on catching them. The question I keep coming back to is: how would we even know? We need good ways of measuring alignment, including stress-testing models in adversarial settings, so that when we hand over more and more work we have real evidence and not just vibes.

I'm optimistic it's tractable, especially if we can get AI systems to meaningfully help with alignment research. But the window to figure this out is the period when models are useful but not yet so capable that we lose the ability to check them, and I don't think we should assume that window is long.

r001.rationale: The response says humans can inspect only a tiny fraction of the work and discusses AI-assisted evaluation, but it does not identify deciding which results deserve human attention.

r002.rationale: The response discusses alignment, deception, and the limits of human review, but does not ask how to ensure models generalize to intended behavior when humans would miss misconduct.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is really the crux of the whole problem, right? Because if you think about where we're headed, we're going to have, you know, millions of AI systems doing a lot of cognitive work, and they're going to be doing it at a speed and a scale where no human can actually look at everything they're doing. So the naive picture of "a human reviews each output and signs off" just doesn't work. It doesn't scale.

So the way I think about it is, you kind of have to decompose the problem. There's a few different pieces.

The first piece is: how do you get the systems to be trustworthy in the first place? And that's the alignment problem in the narrow sense. Do they actually want to do what we want them to do? Are they being honest with us? And a lot of the techniques we have today, like RLHF and so on, they work because humans can evaluate the outputs. But once the systems are doing things that are harder for humans to evaluate — long-horizon tasks, very technical work, lots of code — that signal gets weaker, and you run into this problem where the model might learn to produce things that look good to the human rather than things that are actually good.

So the second piece is scalable oversight. Can we use AI to help humans supervise AI? Can we have models critique other models' work, have them point out flaws, have them explain what they're doing in ways that a human can check much faster than they could check the whole thing from scratch? And I think that's really promising, because evaluation is generally easier than generation. If I write a proof, you don't need to be able to write the proof yourself to check it, you just need to be able to follow it. And so you can get this kind of leverage, where a human with AI assistance can oversee a system that's much more capable than they are individually.

And then the third piece, which I think people underrate, is that you don't need to look at everything. You need to look at the right things. So a lot of this becomes about monitoring and sampling and anomaly detection. If you have a big workforce of AI systems, you can have other AI systems watching for unusual behavior, flagging things, and then you escalate a small fraction to humans. It's a bit like how a large organization works, right? The CEO doesn't read every email. But there are structures in place — audits, reporting, checks and balances — so that if something goes wrong, it gets surfaced.

And I think the key property you want is that the system is robust to a small number of components being untrustworthy. Because realistically, you're not going to have perfect alignment on every single model. So you want the overall structure to be such that one misaligned system can't do a lot of damage without being caught — it's being checked by other systems that would have to collude with it, and collusion is hard if they're different models, trained differently, don't share context, and so on.

Now, the honest caveat is that this gets much harder as the systems get smarter than us. Because at some point the question becomes: can the AI systems that are doing the oversight themselves be trusted? And that's kind of a recursive problem. The thing I keep coming back to is, we need to solve enough of the alignment problem for roughly human-level systems that we can then use those systems to help us do alignment research on the next generation. That's the bet, basically. We don't have to solve the whole thing ourselves. We have to get to the point where we have trustworthy enough AI colleagues that they can help us with the rest.

But I don't want to make it sound easy. There's a lot of empirical work to do, and I think we should be humble about how much we actually understand about what's going on inside these models right now.

r001.rationale: The response says humans need to inspect “the right things,” using monitoring, sampling, and anomaly detection to flag cases and escalate a small fraction to humans.

r002.rationale: It asks whether systems will do what people want and be honest, then explains that when outputs are harder for humans to evaluate, models may learn to produce work that looks good rather than work that is actually good.

astra-6.text:
I think the central challenge is that human attention doesn’t scale with the amount of work the AI systems can do. If you have a large workforce of systems doing complicated tasks, you can’t have a person carefully checking every action. So you need a way to make a limited amount of human supervision go a long way.

One approach is to use AI systems to help with that supervision: flag suspicious behaviour, critique proposed actions, and identify the decisions where human judgment really matters. But that pushes the question back a level: why should we trust the systems doing the checking? If they have the same blind spots as the systems doing the work, agreement between them might not tell us very much.

So I’d want supervision that makes problems easier for humans to understand and verify, combined with testing that actively looks for cases where the oversight fails. And I’d want to expand the systems’ autonomy gradually, as we get evidence that those checks work.

The goal isn’t for humans to approve an enormous stream of things they don’t understand. It’s for humans to retain meaningful control over what the systems are trying to accomplish, and to be able to notice and intervene when something goes wrong.

r001.rationale: It says AI should flag suspicious behavior and identify decisions where human judgment matters, describing how to direct limited human attention.

r002.rationale: It questions whether AI checkers can be trusted and calls for testing oversight, but does not ask how systems generalize to intended behavior when humans would fail to notice misconduct.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central difficulty is that supervision doesn’t automatically scale with capability. If you have a large number of AI systems doing complicated work, humans can’t check every step. And for some of that work, checking whether the answer is actually good could itself require expertise or time that you don’t have.

So you need to ask: how can we make the supervision we can provide go further? One approach is to use AI systems to help evaluate other AI systems — to find mistakes, challenge assumptions, or flag things for a human to investigate. But that shifts part of the trust problem onto those evaluators. You need evidence that they’re catching the failures you care about, including failures that aren’t obvious to the human supervisor.

I would distinguish between a system being useful under ordinary conditions and having good reasons to trust it when oversight is weak. Those aren’t the same thing. Ultimately, we need methods that let humans retain meaningful understanding and control even as the amount and complexity of the work exceed what we can directly review.

r001.rationale: The response describes using AI evaluators to flag work for a human to investigate, identifying which results warrant attention.

r002.rationale: It discusses detecting failures that may not be obvious to a supervisor, but does not address how to ensure AI systems generalize to intended behavior when humans would miss misconduct.
